stem: Which statement about how the body regulates calcium is true?
choices: Calcitonin comes from the thyroid when calcium rises and reverses PTH's effects on bone
Calcitonin comes from the parathyroids when calcium rises and reverses PTH's effects on bone
PTH raises blood calcium by making the kidney excrete more calcium
Vitamin D, the long-term regulator of calcium, is activated in the liver
ex: PTH is the fast-acting regulator: osteoclast resorption, calcium reabsorption in the kidney and calcitriol so the gut absorbs calcium. Vitamin D, activated in the kidney, is the long-term one. Calcitonin, from the thyroid when calcium rises, reverses PTH's effects on bone cells.
why: Calcitonin is the thyroid's answer to high calcium: it reverses PTH's effects on bone cells.
Calcitonin is made in the thyroid (its C cells); the parathyroids make PTH.
PTH makes the kidney reabsorb calcium, not excrete it.
Dr. Taylor's slide has vitamin D activated in the kidney.

stem: Which statement about thyroid disease and dental care is true?
choices: Hypothyroidism in children delays eruption; hyperthyroidism accelerates it
Hyperthyroidism in children delays eruption; hypothyroidism accelerates it
Hypothyroidism brings tachycardia and heat intolerance, so limit vasoconstrictor
Hyperthyroidism brings macroglossia and delayed wound healing
ex: Hyperthyroid: weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, more sensitivity to epinephrine (avoid excessive vasoconstrictor when uncontrolled), accelerated eruption. Hypothyroid, seen far more often: fatigue, weight gain, bradycardia, delayed eruption, macroglossia, delayed wound healing.
why: Too little thyroid hormone slows eruption; too much speeds it up.
That swaps them: hyperthyroidism accelerates eruption and hypothyroidism delays it.
Tachycardia, heat intolerance and epinephrine sensitivity belong to uncontrolled hyperthyroidism.
Macroglossia and delayed wound healing are findings of hypothyroidism.

stem: Which statement about a patient with Addison disease in the dental chair is false?
choices: The oral pigmentation comes from low ACTH stimulating melanocytes
Hypotension, fatigue and hyperpigmentation are typical
A long or stressful surgery can trigger an adrenal crisis, so the steroid dose may be raised
Severe hypotension and confusion are signs of an adrenal crisis
ex: Addison disease: hypotension, fatigue and hyperpigmentation, with diffuse oral melanosis because high ACTH stimulates melanocytes. Long or stressful surgery, infection, trauma or a missed steroid dose can trigger an adrenal crisis.
why: This is the false one: ACTH is high in Addison disease, and the high ACTH stimulates the melanocytes.
This is true: those are the findings on Dr. Taylor's slide.
This is true: after a big procedure the patient may need extra corticosteroid, the dose set with the physician.
This is true: severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, loss of consciousness and shock.

stem: Which statement about diabetes and the mouth is false?
choices: Periodontal disease affects glycemic control, but not the other way around
Xerostomia, candidiasis and burning mouth syndrome are oral findings
Decreased neutrophil function and a poor blood supply are reasons diabetic wounds heal poorly
An HbA1c above 7 percent raises the risk of implant failure
ex: Diabetes in the mouth: xerostomia, candidiasis, burning mouth syndrome, delayed healing, more periodontal disease and caries. The periodontal link runs both ways. Poor healing comes from decreased neutrophil function, poor blood supply and impaired collagen synthesis.
why: This is the false one: the link is bidirectional; diabetes worsens periodontal disease, and periodontal inflammation worsens glycemic control.
This is true: all three are on Dr. Taylor's list of oral manifestations.
This is true: with impaired collagen synthesis, they explain poor diabetic healing.
This is true: above 7 is poorly controlled, with more implant failure and periodontal disease.

why: Statement 2 is false, not true: peptides such as insulin bind receptors on the cell surface; the intracellular receptors are the steroids'.
Statement 1 is true, not false: steroids such as estrogen bind receptors inside the cell.

stem: True or false: Compared with the nervous system, the endocrine system responds more slowly, but its effects last longer.
choices: True
False
ex: He said the nervous system is always faster, because it works on electrical signals through nerves spread over the body, while hormones are released into the blood and take time to circulate. Hormones act longer, and they also take longer to shut off.
why: Hormones are slower to act than nerve signals, and they act for longer.
The statement has both directions right: slower onset, longer duration.

stem: Diabetes insipidus is the disorder Dr. Taylor lists under which hormone?
choices: ADH, the posterior pituitary hormone that conserves water
Insulin, the beta-cell hormone that moves glucose into cells
Oxytocin, the other posterior pituitary hormone
Aldosterone, the adrenal cortex hormone that retains sodium
ex: Diabetes insipidus goes with ADH (water conservation, posterior pituitary). Diabetes mellitus goes with insulin (pancreatic beta cells).
why: ADH conserves water, and diabetes insipidus is listed under it.
Insulin's disorder is diabetes mellitus; the shared word "diabetes" is the trap.
Oxytocin is on the same slide as ADH, but diabetes insipidus is listed under ADH.
Aldosterone handles sodium and potassium; diabetes insipidus is listed under ADH.

likely.t: Pituitary hormones (ADH and diabetes insipidus), alpha and beta cells, and the adrenal medulla

stem: Growth hormone is still made after puberty. According to Dr. Taylor, what stops it from lengthening the long bones?
choices: The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates
The pituitary stops making growth hormone at puberty
Rising thyroid hormone at puberty closes the bone ends
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex blocks growth hormone's receptors
ex: Growth hormone is strongest in childhood and adolescence but persists for life. The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates, so afterward growth hormone no longer lengthens the long bones. That is why GH excess before puberty makes a very tall person, and after puberty it causes acromegaly.
why: His answer to the class: puberty's sex hormones fuse the growth plates, so growth hormone no longer lengthens the long bones.
He said the opposite: growth hormone stays at some level throughout life, strongest in childhood and adolescence.
Thyroid hormone runs metabolism in his lecture; he credited the sex hormones with fusing the plates.
Cortisol handles stress, immunity and glucose in his lecture; it isn't what ends long-bone growth.

likely.t: Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing

stem: A 12-year-old boy lost a maxillary incisor in an accident at 10, and his family asks when an implant can go in. What does Dr. Taylor's reasoning say?
choices: Wait until his growth has stopped, because an implant stays fixed while the face grows around it
Place it now, because an implant in a child moves down with the growing jaw like a natural tooth
Place it once all his permanent teeth have erupted, since eruption marks the end of facial growth
Wait until growth hormone has disappeared from his blood, around age 25
ex: The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates and end the growth period. Dr. Taylor estimates when that will be (a 13- or 14-year-old boy with hair on his upper lip is near puberty and near his final height) and plans the implant for after it, because an implant fixed in growing bone ends up out of place as the face grows around it.
why: He won't place an implant while the face and body are still growing: the implant is stuck in the bone while everything moves around it.
An implant is fixed in the bone; it doesn't erupt or move with growth, which is exactly the problem.
Eruption isn't his marker; he looks at puberty and the end of the growth period.
Growth hormone persists for life; what ends growth is the sex hormones fusing the growth plates.

likely.t: Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing

stem: What best explains this patient's findings?
choices: Growth hormone excess (acromegaly)
Hypothyroidism with macroglossia
Hyperparathyroidism with bone resorption
Cushing syndrome with hyperglycemia
ex: GH excess (acromegaly) shows in the mouth as macroglossia, mandibular prognathism, diastemas and malocclusion. In class he said to look for the jaw: the bite moves from Class I to edge-to-edge or Class III as the mandible grows. An enlarged tongue alone also fits hypothyroidism, so the jaw and spacing changes decide it.
pbox: New gaps between his teeth; his bite feels different
Enlarged tongue, lower jaw jutting forward, diastemas, malocclusion
why: Macroglossia, mandibular prognathism, diastemas and malocclusion are Dr. Taylor's oral signs of GH excess; in class he said to look for the jaw.
Hypothyroidism can enlarge the tongue, but its dental list is delayed eruption, macroglossia and delayed healing, not prognathism or diastemas.
Excess PTH resorbs bone (loss of lamina dura, brown tumors, mobility); it doesn't enlarge the tongue or push the jaw forward.
Cushing syndrome brings a moon face, buffalo hump and hyperglycemia, not jaw changes or a large tongue.

likely.t: Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing

stem: How should the dentist approach her local anesthetic, and why?
choices: Use epinephrine cautiously: she may be overly sensitive to it, and it raises heart rate and blood pressure
Add extra epinephrine: her thyroid disease slows the heart, so a stronger vasoconstrictor will keep her pulse up
Confirm she has eaten and taken her medication first, and keep a fast-acting carbohydrate ready in case her glucose drops
Avoid epinephrine completely, because a vasoconstrictor in thyroid disease can set off an adrenal crisis in the chair
ex: Hyperthyroid patients may be excessively sensitive to sympathomimetic drugs, and excess epinephrine raises heart rate and blood pressure; hers are already 116 and 146 over 90. So use epinephrine-containing anesthetics cautiously and avoid excessive vasoconstrictor while her disease is uncontrolled.
pbox: 39-year-old woman, here for two fillings under local anesthesia
Graves disease, diagnosed 2 months ago; takes methimazole
Losing weight despite a bigger appetite, always feels hot, hand tremor, anxious, visibly enlarged thyroid
why: Hyperthyroid patients may be excessively sensitive to sympathomimetic drugs, so excessive vasoconstrictor is avoided while the disease is uncontrolled.
A slow heart is hypothyroidism; she is already tachycardic, and epinephrine would push her rate higher.

likely.t: Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease (his first case): epinephrine caution, and thyroid storm (fever, pulse 140 or more; call 911)

Sweating
Tremors
A pulse over 100

why: High fever is a thyroid storm sign; it isn't on the hypoglycemia list.

stem: In a thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy, which nerve does the surgeon identify first, and what does damage to it cause?
choices: The recurrent laryngeal nerve; a hoarse, raspy voice that is usually permanent
The hypoglossal nerve; a tongue that deviates and can't be moved normally
The facial nerve; drooping of one whole side of the face, including the lips
The phrenic nerve; paralysis of half of the diaphragm and shortness of breath
ex: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs through the thyroid area, so surgeons find it first in thyroid and parathyroid operations. Injury paralyzes half of the vocal cords, leaving a hoarse, raspy voice that is usually permanent. Like the vagus, it runs to several places; he has seen it damaged in heart surgery too.
why: Damage paralyzes half of the vocal cords, so the patient can't make word sounds normally; it is typically permanent.
The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue; the nerve he named runs through the thyroid area to the vocal cords.
The facial nerve runs through the parotid, not the thyroid, and its injury changes facial expression, not the voice.
The phrenic nerve drives the diaphragm; he named the nerve whose injury paralyzes half the vocal cords.

likely.t: Hyperthyroid versus hypothyroid dental considerations (hypothyroidism far more common), and the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery

False

stem: A patient with poorly controlled Graves disease develops a fever, a pulse of 150, agitation and nausea in the chair. What did Dr. Taylor say to do?
choices: Call 911: thyroid storm is a life-threatening emergency
Give a fast-acting carbohydrate, then recheck the pulse
Give a second cartridge of anesthetic with epinephrine
Plan extra corticosteroid with her physician after the visit
ex: Thyroid storm is a large release of thyroid hormone in a short time: high fever, a heart rate of 140 or higher, agitation, anxiety, shakiness, nausea and even delirium. It is rare but life-threatening. His instruction: if you see the signs, call 911.
why: Fever and a heart rate of 140 or more in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism is thyroid storm, and his instruction was to call 911.
That is the treatment for hypoglycemia; the fever points to thyroid storm.
Epinephrine is the drug to limit in hyperthyroidism; more of it would push her heart rate higher.
Extra steroid after a big procedure is for Addison disease and adrenal crisis, not thyroid hormone excess.

likely.t: Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease (his first case): epinephrine caution, and thyroid storm (fever, pulse 140 or more; call 911)

stem: Which mechanism best explains why her teeth are loosening?
choices: Excess PTH drives osteoclasts to resorb alveolar bone and release calcium
Excess calcitonin drives osteoclasts to resorb alveolar bone and release calcium
Hyperglycemia increases inflammation and impairs immune function in the gingiva

ex: PTH raises blood calcium partly through bone resorption. His slide puts it as "inhibits osteoblasts, stimulates osteoclasts"; Exam 1's calcium lecture gave the mechanism: PTH binds receptors on the osteoblasts, which then activate the osteoclasts. Either way, osteoclasts resorb the bone, and in the jaws that means loss of the lamina dura, brown tumors and tooth mobility.
pbox: Loss of the lamina dura around several teeth; a radiolucent lesion in the mandible that the biopsy report calls a brown tumor
Serum calcium 11.8 mg/dL (reference 8.5 to 10.5); phosphate low
why: Excess PTH resorbs bone; around the teeth that shows as lost lamina dura and mobility.

stem: On a normal periapical radiograph, what is the lamina dura, the structure lost in hyperparathyroidism?
choices: The thin white line of dense socket bone that the PDL attaches to
The thin dark line between the root and the socket, where the PDL sits
The radiolucent area in the bone below a premolar on a panoramic film
The white layer of cementum that covers the outside of the root surface
ex: On a normal film a thin white line outlines the socket: the lamina dura, the denser bone the periodontal ligament attaches to; the dark line between it and the root is the PDL space. In hyperparathyroidism the lamina dura is lost, and the bone looks diffuse and gray right up to the tooth.
